content: Essential interventions for infants under six months of age with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) include specific feeding approaches. These approaches aim to address the unique nutritional and physiological needs of this vulnerable age group. Criteria for transferring infants under six months of age with SAM from inpatient hospital care to outpatient care, or for discharging them from treatment, include the resolution of all clinical conditions or medical complications (including edema), the presence of a good appetite, clinical wellness and alertness, and adequate weight gain. Additionally, the infant should have received all necessary immunizations and routine interventions, and caregivers should be linked to community-based follow-up and support systems. Systematic reviews were conducted to evaluate admission and discharge criteria for managing infants under six months of age with SAM. However, no studies were identified that directly examined these criteria using WHO growth standards. Similarly, no peer-reviewed studies reported outcomes when WHO therapeutic feeding recommendations for older children with SAM were applied to infants under six months of age. Some studies included infants under six months of age in their examination of therapeutic feeding approaches. However, subgroup analyses specific to this age group were not feasible due to small sample sizes or insufficient treatment details. A randomized controlled trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo recruited 161 infants under six months of age with SAM, defined as weight-for-length less than 70% of the median NCHS reference values and without edema. Infants who were not gaining weight at home, were too weak to breastfeed, or whose mothers reported an inability to breastfeed were also included. Infants were provided with the same treatment protocols, which included support for continued breastfeeding, supplemental sucking when needed, and administration of vitamins, folic acid, and antibiotics. Diluted F-100 or generic infant formula milk was used as a supplement, with volumes reduced by half when the infant gained at least 20 g/day for three consecutive days and stopped entirely when weight gain was maintained at 10 g/day. No significant differences were observed in weight gain, total treatment duration, or treatment outcomes (death, recovery, or default). A doctoral thesis reported the use of WHO therapeutic feeding protocols for older children (6–59 months) applied to infants under six months of age. Infants from 13 African countries were admitted for SAM treatment, identified by weight-for-length <70% of the median reference value (NCHS). Infants under six months of age had higher mortality rates, particularly those who were not breastfed, compared to older children treated with the same protocol. Attempts to breastfeed infants up to 24 times a day were abandoned due to rapid weight loss. The supplemental sucking technique was successfully introduced to feed these infants. Increased mortality was attributed to the use of undiluted F-100, which resulted in a high renal solute load. No studies examined feeding approaches during the transition and rehabilitation phases of SAM treatment in infants under six months of age. Some national guidelines include supplemental sucking treatment as part of care for these infants, with the volume of supplemental milk gradually reduced and eventually stopped as the infant improves and breast milk supply is re-established. However, this practice has not been explicitly referred to as transitioning to a rehabilitation phase. No references were found regarding the use of cup or spoon feeding in the context of young infants with SAM, although their effectiveness has been demonstrated in other settings for young children without SAM. The overall quality of evidence has been rated as very low due to indirectness and imprecision. The guideline development group emphasized the importance of programmatic guidance for healthcare workers treating SAM in this age group. They highlighted the relevance of general nutritional and infant feeding principles and their application to young infants with SAM. The group also acknowledged the value of existing WHO recommendations, such as those for feeding non-breastfed children aged 6–24 months and the integrated course on infant and young child feeding. The use of the 2011 WHO growth velocity standards and the assessment of growth velocity (weight) was considered equally or more important than a single weight-for-length value. This underscores the importance of maintaining and examining growth-monitoring charts at the primary healthcare level for infants and young children. As with older children, SAM in infants under six months of age can be classified as uncomplicated or complicated. These infants should be managed in outpatient or inpatient settings, respectively. The potential benefits of inpatient treatment should be carefully weighed against the risks, particularly nosocomial infections. The guideline development group acknowledged that generic infant formula milk can be safely provided in some inpatient settings. However, mothers or caregivers expected to provide formula milk after discharge need clear guidance on safe preparation and use. This information is included in the WHO integrated course on infant and young child feeding. The group also emphasized that formula milk programs should not compromise public health messages promoting exclusive breastfeeding for infants under six months of age. Participants of a 2004 WHO meeting concluded that young infants with edema should be fed with F-75 during the stabilization phase. In contrast, F-75 was deemed inappropriate for severely wasted infants without edema, for whom generic infant formula or diluted F-100 would be safer. However, no data were presented to substantiate these conclusions. The meeting report described diverse opinions on feeding strategies for the rehabilitation phase. There was consensus that infants under six months of age with SAM should not be given undiluted F-100 due to the high renal solute load and risk of hypernatremic dehydration. Infants in this age group have small daily weight gains that require precise scales with at least 20 g accuracy for monitoring. In some settings, ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) is being given to infants aged 5–6 months as a pragmatic response when exclusive breastfeeding is not possible or is difficult. However, there is no evaluated evidence to indicate the safety or effectiveness of this approach. An urgent research agenda has been identified to address these gaps. Relevant standing recommendations include those outlined in the WHO Management of Severe Malnutrition manual (1999) and the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines (2000). SAM in infants aged 0–5 months is defined as weight-for-length less than –3 Z-score or the presence of bilateral pitting edema. Infants with poor weight gain who do not respond to nutritional counseling and support should be admitted for further investigation and treatment. Infants with general danger signs, such as inability to drink or breastfeed, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargy, or unconsciousness, should be admitted for urgent care. Infants under six months of age with SAM and complicating factors, such as serious clinical conditions, recent weight loss, ineffective feeding, pitting edema, or adverse social circumstances, should be admitted for inpatient care. Feeding approaches should prioritize establishing or re-establishing effective exclusive breastfeeding. If breastfeeding is not possible, appropriate replacement feeds, such as generic infant formula, should be provided with relevant support for safe preparation and use. Infants admitted to inpatient care can be transferred to outpatient care when all clinical conditions are resolved, they have a good appetite, are clinically well and alert, and demonstrate adequate weight gain. They should also have received all immunizations and routine interventions, and caregivers should be linked to community-based follow-up and support. Infants can be discharged from all care when they are breastfeeding effectively or feeding well with replacement feeds, have adequate weight gain, and achieve a weight-for-length ≥ –2 Z-score. The guideline group noted that while the quality of evidence is very low, the recommendations should remain strong. Most recommendations reflect standard care practices and align with other WHO guidelines.
